text: Several conditions specifically disrupt egg production and quality. Infectious Bronchitis: egg production drops (more than 50%) around the same time as respiratory signs, recovering after 5–6 weeks but at a lower rate; eggs may be soft-shelled, deformed, or watery inside; ovarian hemorrhages and yellow abdominal fluid (yolk material) can be found at necropsy; birds infected with IB in their first week of life may never become good layers due to oviduct damage. Calcium deficiency: a pullet's calcium needs jump roughly fourfold (to about 4 g/day) once she starts laying; insufficient calcium reduces egg output and shell quality (thin, soft shells); hens draw down bone calcium reserves when deficient, leading to brittle bones and, in severe cases, inability to stand — supplement with DCP or oyster shell. Mycotoxins: fungi grow on feed ingredients (especially corn) above 12% moisture and produce toxins that are invisible without lab testing; ducks are more sensitive than chickens; acute cases can cause up to 50% mortality, with lowered disease resistance and a sharp drop in egg production even in milder cases — prevention means buying good-quality, properly dried corn, and binding agents (e.g. 'Detox' clay products, 100–200 g per 100 kg of feed) can adsorb mycotoxins already present. Lice: scratching from heavy lice infestation can cut egg production up to 20%; controlled with Carbaryl (twice, 4 weeks apart), though Carbaryl must never be used on layers whose eggs are sold for human consumption. Worms: Ascaris, the most common poultry roundworm, may not cause major mortality but even mild-to-severe infestation slows growth and reduces egg output. Newcastle Disease: a prolonged, dramatic egg-production drop can occur with a lingering infection (often alongside neck-twisting signs), with ovarian follicle hemorrhages found at necropsy. Lymphoid Leukosis: a viral disease occurring during laying in birds over 6 months old, causing reduced feed intake and complete cessation of egg laying, with tumors of the liver, spleen, bursa, and ovary found at necropsy.
